_meta.description: Human-readable content for each finding type. Kept separate from scanner logic so security engineers or technical writers can update titles, descriptions, and remediation guidance without touching Python code. Content is loaded by app.scanners.content_loader and used by the scanner rules to construct Finding objects.

field_notes.title: Short heading, sentence case, under 60 characters.
field_notes.severity: One of low, medium, high, critical. Must match app.models.finding.Severity.
field_notes.description: Plain-English explanation of WHY the misconfiguration matters. Should be defensible to an auditor and include real-world context where possible.
field_notes.remediation: Action-focused fix guidance. Include both AWS Console click-path AND AWS CLI command, so both audiences can use it. Use placeholder <name> where the specific bucket name would go.

S3_PUBLIC_VIA_ACL.title: Bucket publicly readable via legacy ACL
S3_PUBLIC_VIA_ACL.description: The bucket ACL grants the AllUsers group read permission, exposing every object to anyone on the internet without authentication. This is the single most common cause of accidental S3 data leaks; historical incidents at Verizon, Accenture, and Booz Allen Hamilton all traced back to this misconfiguration. Because ACLs predate bucket policies and IAM, they are easy to leave in place unnoticed on older buckets.
S3_PUBLIC_VIA_ACL.remediation: Remove the AllUsers grant. In the AWS Console: S3 -> the bucket -> Permissions tab -> Access Control List -> Edit -> uncheck all 'Everyone (public access)' boxes -> Save. From the AWS CLI: `aws s3api put-bucket-acl --bucket <name> --acl private`. Verify with `aws s3api get-bucket-acl --bucket <name>` and confirm no Grantee with URI 'http://acs.amazonaws.com/groups/global/AllUsers' appears in the output.

S3_PUBLIC_ACCESS_BLOCK_DISABLED.title: S3 Public Access Block not fully enabled
S3_PUBLIC_ACCESS_BLOCK_DISABLED.description: AWS Public Access Block is the account-and-bucket-level safety net that overrides accidentally-public ACLs and bucket policies before they can expose data. One or more of the four flags (BlockPublicAcls, IgnorePublicAcls, BlockPublicPolicy, RestrictPublicBuckets) is disabled, meaning a future ACL or policy mistake would not be caught automatically. This does not mean the bucket is currently public, but it does mean the safety net protecting future changes has a hole in it.
S3_PUBLIC_ACCESS_BLOCK_DISABLED.remediation: Enable all four Public Access Block flags. In the AWS Console: S3 -> the bucket -> Permissions tab -> Block public access -> Edit -> check 'Block all public access' -> Save. From the AWS CLI: `aws s3api put-public-access-block --bucket <name> --public-access-block-configuration BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true`. Buckets that legitimately serve public content should do so via CloudFront with an Origin Access Identity, not by leaving the bucket world-readable.

S3_ENCRYPTION_DISABLED.title: Server-side encryption not configured
S3_ENCRYPTION_DISABLED.description: Objects in this bucket are stored unencrypted at rest. AWS enables default AES256 encryption automatically on all new buckets created after January 2023, so an unencrypted bucket typically indicates either an older bucket that predates the automatic default, or an explicit misconfiguration. Regulated data such as customer PII, financial records, and health records must be encrypted at rest under UK GDPR, PCI DSS, and HIPAA. Even for non-regulated data, encryption at rest is a baseline expectation of the ICO's Data Protection by Design principle.
S3_ENCRYPTION_DISABLED.remediation: Enable server-side encryption on the bucket. In the AWS Console: S3 -> the bucket -> Properties tab -> Default encryption -> Edit -> choose 'Server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3)' for AES256, or 'Server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS)' for compliance-sensitive data -> Save. From the AWS CLI: `aws s3api put-bucket-encryption --bucket <name> --server-side-encryption-configuration '{"Rules":[{"ApplyServerSideEncryptionByDefault":{"SSEAlgorithm":"AES256"}}]}'`. New objects uploaded after this change will be encrypted automatically; existing objects need to be copied over themselves (aws s3 cp) to acquire the new encryption.

S3_ENCRYPTION_NOT_DEDICATED_KMS_KEY.title: Bucket not encrypted with a dedicated KMS key
S3_ENCRYPTION_NOT_DEDICATED_KMS_KEY.description: This bucket is encrypted, but not with a customer-managed KMS key created specifically for it -- it's using either SSE-S3 (Amazon's own managed key, AES256) or SSE-KMS with the account's shared AWS-managed default key (aws/s3). Both protect data at rest, but neither gives you the controls a dedicated customer-managed key does: you can't write a key policy scoping who's allowed to decrypt, you can't disable or schedule deletion of the key independently of the bucket, and CloudTrail can't show you who used the key to decrypt what, since the AWS-managed key is shared across every bucket that defaults to it, not specific to this one.
S3_ENCRYPTION_NOT_DEDICATED_KMS_KEY.remediation: Create (or reuse) a customer-managed KMS key dedicated to this bucket's data, then point the bucket's default encryption at it. In the AWS Console: KMS -> Create key (if needed), then S3 -> the bucket -> Properties -> Default encryption -> Edit -> 'Server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS)' -> choose the customer-managed key -> Save. From the CLI: `aws s3api put-bucket-encryption --bucket <name> --server-side-encryption-configuration '{"Rules":[{"ApplyServerSideEncryptionByDefault":{"SSEAlgorithm":"aws:kms","KMSMasterKeyID":"<key-arn>"}}]}'`.

S3_VERSIONING_DISABLED.title: Bucket versioning not enabled
S3_VERSIONING_DISABLED.description: This bucket has never had versioning turned on, so deleting or overwriting an object destroys the previous copy permanently. Versioning is S3's built-in defence against accidental deletion, application bugs that overwrite data, and ransomware-style mass-encryption of objects: with it enabled, every prior version remains recoverable. It also underpins MFA Delete and object-level recovery workflows that many incident response runbooks assume are available.
S3_VERSIONING_DISABLED.remediation: Enable versioning on the bucket. In the AWS Console: S3 -> the bucket -> Properties tab -> Bucket Versioning -> Edit -> select 'Enable' -> Save. From the AWS CLI: `aws s3api put-bucket-versioning --bucket <name> --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled`. Verify with `aws s3api get-bucket-versioning --bucket <name>` and confirm the Status is 'Enabled'. Once enabled, versioning cannot be fully turned off again, only suspended, so pair this with a lifecycle rule to expire old versions and control storage cost.

S3_LOGGING_DISABLED.title: S3 access logging not enabled
S3_LOGGING_DISABLED.description: Server access logging has never been configured for this bucket, so there is no record of who requested which object, when, from where, or whether the request succeeded. Without it, investigating a suspected data exposure means answering 'what was accessed and by whom' with no data to draw on. Access logs are also frequently requested as evidence during an audit or incident response, separate from CloudTrail, which logs API management events rather than individual object-level GET/PUT requests.
S3_LOGGING_DISABLED.remediation: Enable server access logging, pointing at a separate logging bucket (never the bucket itself, to avoid a logging loop). In the AWS Console: S3 -> the bucket -> Properties tab -> Server access logging -> Edit -> Enable -> choose a target bucket and prefix -> Save. From the AWS CLI: `aws s3api put-bucket-logging --bucket <name> --bucket-logging-status '{"LoggingEnabled":{"TargetBucket":"<log-bucket>","TargetPrefix":"<name>/"}}'`. The target bucket needs the standard S3 log-delivery ACL grant, which the Console option configures automatically.

S3_LIFECYCLE_MISSING.title: S3 lifecycle policy not configured
S3_LIFECYCLE_MISSING.description: This bucket has no lifecycle rules, so objects accumulate indefinitely with no automatic expiration, transition to cheaper storage, or cleanup of old versions. Beyond the storage cost of keeping data nobody is using, unbounded retention runs against data minimisation expectations under UK GDPR and increases how much is exposed if the bucket is ever compromised: there is simply more data sitting there to find. A defined retention period is increasingly something regulators and auditors expect to see documented, not assumed.
S3_LIFECYCLE_MISSING.remediation: Add a lifecycle rule appropriate to the data in the bucket. In the AWS Console: S3 -> the bucket -> Management tab -> Lifecycle rules -> Create lifecycle rule -> set an expiration (and, for versioned buckets, a noncurrent version expiration) -> Save. From the AWS CLI: `aws s3api put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration --bucket <name> --lifecycle-configuration '{"Rules":[{"ID":"expire-old-objects","Status":"Enabled","Filter":{"Prefix":""},"Expiration":{"Days":365}}]}'`. Set the expiration window to match the organisation's actual data retention policy rather than an arbitrary default.

S3_TLS_NOT_ENFORCED.title: Bucket policy does not enforce TLS
S3_TLS_NOT_ENFORCED.description: This bucket has no policy statement denying requests made over plain HTTP, so requests to it are not required to use TLS. AWS's S3 API endpoints support both HTTP and HTTPS by default; without an explicit deny, a misconfigured client, an old script, or a tool that silently falls back to HTTP would transmit object data and credentials in the request unencrypted, exposed to anyone positioned on the network path. This is a policy-level gap rather than a data-at-rest gap: it exists even on buckets where server-side encryption is otherwise correctly configured.
S3_TLS_NOT_ENFORCED.remediation: Add a bucket policy statement that denies any request where aws:SecureTransport is false. In the AWS Console: S3 -> the bucket -> Permissions tab -> Bucket policy -> Edit -> add the statement below -> Save. From the AWS CLI: `aws s3api put-bucket-policy --bucket <name> --policy '{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Sid":"DenyInsecureTransport","Effect":"Deny","Principal":"*","Action":"s3:*","Resource":["arn:aws:s3:::<name>","arn:aws:s3:::<name>/*"],"Condition":{"Bool":{"aws:SecureTransport":"false"}}}]}'`. If the bucket already has a policy, merge this statement into the existing Statement array rather than overwriting it.

KMS_KEY_ROTATION_DISABLED.title: KMS key rotation not enabled
KMS_KEY_ROTATION_DISABLED.description: This customer-managed KMS key does not have automatic annual rotation enabled. Without rotation, the same underlying cryptographic material continues protecting data indefinitely; if the key material were ever compromised, everything it has ever encrypted stays exposed with no way to limit the blast radius to a shorter window. Enabling rotation is a single setting with no application-level impact, since KMS keeps prior key material available to decrypt data that was encrypted under it, so there is no practical downside to leaving it off other than an unnecessarily wide exposure window. This finding only applies to customer-managed keys: AWS-managed keys (for example the default aws/s3 key) rotate automatically every year with no action available to the account owner, so they are excluded from this check rather than flagged for a setting nobody can change.
KMS_KEY_ROTATION_DISABLED.remediation: Enable automatic key rotation. In the AWS Console: KMS -> Customer managed keys -> select the key -> Key rotation tab -> Enable automatic key rotation -> Save. From the AWS CLI: `aws kms enable-key-rotation --key-id <key-id>`. Verify with `aws kms get-key-rotation-status --key-id <key-id>` and confirm KeyRotationEnabled is true. Rotation happens automatically once a year after this is enabled; no further action or re-encryption of existing data is required.

KMS_KEY_PENDING_DELETION.title: KMS key scheduled for deletion
KMS_KEY_PENDING_DELETION.description: This customer-managed KMS key has been scheduled for deletion. Once the waiting period (7 to 30 days, set at schedule time) elapses, AWS permanently destroys the key material, and every object, secret, or volume encrypted under it becomes permanently unrecoverable with no way to reverse the action, even for AWS. This is functionally identical to deleting the data itself, but far easier to do by accident: a deletion schedule can be set with a single API call or console click, often without the caller realising what else depends on the key. Attackers have also used key deletion deliberately as a destructive technique against S3-encrypted data, since it destroys everything the key protects without touching the objects themselves.
KMS_KEY_PENDING_DELETION.remediation: If this deletion was not intentional, cancel it immediately: in the AWS Console, KMS -> Customer managed keys -> select the key -> Key actions -> Cancel key deletion, or from the CLI, `aws kms cancel-key-deletion --key-id <key-id>`. Before deleting a key on purpose, confirm nothing still depends on it: check CloudTrail for recent Decrypt/GenerateDataKey calls against the key, and check every S3 bucket, EBS volume, and Secrets Manager secret that lists it as their encryption key. There is no undo once the waiting period expires.

IAM_ROOT_ACCESS_KEYS_ACTIVE.title: Root user has active access keys
IAM_ROOT_ACCESS_KEYS_ACTIVE.description: The account's root user has one or more active access keys. Root has no permissions boundary: it bypasses every IAM policy, every SCP, and every permissions boundary in the account, and it cannot be restricted the way an IAM user or role can. There is no legitimate day-to-day workflow that needs root API access; AWS's own guidance is that root credentials should be locked away and used only for the handful of account-level tasks that specifically require them. An active root access key is a standing, unrestrictable credential that, if leaked, gives an attacker complete and immediate control of the account with no IAM guardrail able to stop them.
IAM_ROOT_ACCESS_KEYS_ACTIVE.remediation: Deactivate and delete the root access keys. Sign in as root, go to My Security Credentials -> Access keys, and deactivate then delete each key listed there. This must be done via the AWS Management Console or CLI using root's own session; it cannot be done by an IAM user, even an administrator, since nobody else has permission to manage root's credentials. Going forward, root should not have access keys at all: use IAM users or roles with least-privilege policies for every programmatic task, and enable MFA on the root user itself.

IAM_ACCOUNT_MFA_NOT_ENABLED.title: Root user does not have MFA enabled
IAM_ACCOUNT_MFA_NOT_ENABLED.description: The account's root user can sign in with just a password, no second factor required. Root cannot be restricted by any IAM policy or SCP, so a leaked or guessed root password alone is enough for complete account takeover, with no additional barrier. This is one of the first checks in almost every cloud security audit and compliance framework, precisely because it is cheap to fix and catastrophic to leave open: a single reused or phished password becomes full administrative control of every resource in the account.
IAM_ACCOUNT_MFA_NOT_ENABLED.remediation: Enable MFA on the root user. Sign in as root, go to My Security Credentials -> Multi-factor authentication (MFA) -> Assign MFA device, and register a virtual MFA app, hardware key, or FIDO security key. This can only be configured by root itself, in the same way root's access keys can only be managed by root. A hardware or FIDO key is preferable to a virtual authenticator app for the root user specifically, since it removes the phone or app as a single point of failure for the account's highest-privilege identity.

IAM_PASSWORD_POLICY_WEAK.title: Account password policy is weak or missing
IAM_PASSWORD_POLICY_WEAK.description: The account has no password policy configured, or one that allows passwords shorter than 14 characters. AWS applies no minimum length or complexity requirement by default; without an explicit policy, IAM users can set passwords as short and simple as the service allows, which makes every human-authenticated identity in the account an easier target for password guessing and credential-stuffing attacks. A 14-character minimum is the current NCSC and NIST baseline recommendation, and is enforced account-wide with a single setting.
IAM_PASSWORD_POLICY_WEAK.remediation: Set an account password policy with a minimum length of 14 characters. In the AWS Console: IAM -> Account settings -> Password policy -> Edit -> set Minimum password length to 14, and enable password reuse prevention and expiration if the organisation's policy requires it -> Save. From the AWS CLI: `aws iam update-account-password-policy --minimum-password-length 14`. This applies to every IAM user's console password account-wide; it does not affect access keys or MFA, which are separate controls.

IAM_ACCESS_KEY_AGE_EXCEEDS_90_DAYS.title: IAM access key older than 90 days
IAM_ACCESS_KEY_AGE_EXCEEDS_90_DAYS.description: This user has an active access key that was created more than 90 days ago and has never been rotated. Access keys don't expire on their own, so a key created years ago for a one-off task can remain fully valid indefinitely if nobody remembers to remove it. The longer a key lives, the more places it tends to end up copied into (scripts, CI pipelines, developer laptops, old backups), and the larger the window becomes for it to leak without anyone noticing. Rotating keys on a schedule limits how much damage a single leaked credential can do, regardless of when or how it leaked.
IAM_ACCESS_KEY_AGE_EXCEEDS_90_DAYS.remediation: Rotate the key: create a new access key for the user, update every script, application, or CI pipeline that references the old one, verify nothing is still using it (check CloudTrail for recent activity on the old key), then deactivate and delete the old key. In the AWS Console: IAM -> Users -> the user -> Security credentials tab -> Access keys. From the CLI: `aws iam create-access-key --user-name <name>` followed later by `aws iam delete-access-key --user-name <name> --access-key-id <old-key-id>`. If the key isn't actually needed any more, delete it outright rather than rotating it — the best-rotated key is one that doesn't exist.

IAM_CONSOLE_LOGIN_ENABLED.title: IAM user has a console login profile
IAM_CONSOLE_LOGIN_ENABLED.description: This user has a password configured for console access, giving it two separate ways into the account (password login and, potentially, access keys) instead of one. Every IAM user in this account is a service or application identity used by code, not a person sitting at a keyboard -- a console login profile on a credential like this is attack surface nobody needs: a leaked or guessed password becomes a direct path into the AWS Console, bypassing whatever discipline governs the programmatic access keys. Programmatic-only credentials should stay programmatic-only.
IAM_CONSOLE_LOGIN_ENABLED.remediation: Delete the console login profile so this identity can only be used programmatically. In the AWS Console: IAM -> Users -> the user -> Security credentials tab -> Console sign-in -> Manage -> Disable, or delete the login profile outright. From the CLI: `aws iam delete-login-profile --user-name <name>`. Confirm nothing legitimately depends on console access for this identity before removing it -- if a person actually needs console access, that person should have their own IAM user or federated identity, not share this one.

KMS_KEY_MISSING_ALIAS.title: KMS key has no alias pointing to it
KMS_KEY_MISSING_ALIAS.description: This customer-managed key has no alias associated with it. Aliases exist precisely so that infrastructure code, IAM policies, and operators can reference a key by a stable, human-readable name (alias/whatever-this-key-is-for) instead of a raw key ID or ARN that reveals nothing about the key's purpose. A key with no alias is harder to identify safely during an incident, easier to reference by the wrong ID by mistake, and if an alias that used to point here was ever moved to a different key, this is exactly what that drift looks like from the outside.
KMS_KEY_MISSING_ALIAS.remediation: Create an alias that describes what the key protects: in the AWS Console, KMS -> Customer managed keys -> select the key -> Aliases -> Add alias, or from the CLI, `aws kms create-alias --alias-name alias/<descriptive-name> --target-key-id <key-id>`. If an alias was recently repointed away from this key on purpose, confirm that was intentional and that whatever used to reference this key by its old alias has been updated to use the key ID or ARN directly, or a new alias, instead.

IAM_MULTIPLE_ACTIVE_ACCESS_KEYS.title: IAM user has more than one active access key
IAM_MULTIPLE_ACTIVE_ACCESS_KEYS.description: This user has two or more Active access keys at the same time. AWS allows this deliberately so a key rotation can overlap briefly -- create the replacement, migrate everything to it, then deactivate the old one -- but a scan can't tell 'mid-rotation, about to be cleaned up' apart from 'rotation started and never finished'. Every extra live credential is another copy of long-term access sitting somewhere, another thing that can leak, and another key an attacker only needs to find one of.
IAM_MULTIPLE_ACTIVE_ACCESS_KEYS.remediation: Confirm which key is actually in use, then deactivate and delete the other one: `aws iam list-access-keys --user-name <name>` to see both, check recent usage with `aws iam get-access-key-last-used --access-key-id <id>` for each, then `aws iam update-access-key --user-name <name> --access-key-id <old-id> --status Inactive` followed by `aws iam delete-access-key --user-name <name> --access-key-id <old-id>` once you're confident nothing still depends on it.

RESOURCE_MISSING_TAGS.title: Resource has no tags
RESOURCE_MISSING_TAGS.description: This resource has no tags at all. Tags are how resources get attributed to a project, an owner, or a cost centre, and how a tag-based security scan finds what belongs to which project in the first place. An untagged resource is invisible to any scan scoped to a specific project's tag -- not flagged, not skipped, genuinely absent from the results, indistinguishable from a resource that was never created. That's a real blind spot: something could sit here unmonitored indefinitely simply because nobody tagged it.
RESOURCE_MISSING_TAGS.remediation: Add at minimum a Project tag identifying which project or team owns this resource. In the AWS Console: select the resource -> Tags tab -> Manage tags -> Add tag. From the CLI, the exact command depends on the resource type, e.g. `aws s3api put-bucket-tagging`, `aws kms tag-resource`, or `aws iam tag-user`. If this resource genuinely belongs to no active project, consider whether it should still exist at all.

ACCOUNT_CLOUDTRAIL_DISABLED.title: No active CloudTrail trail logging the account
ACCOUNT_CLOUDTRAIL_DISABLED.description: This account has no CloudTrail trail configured, or every trail that exists is not currently logging. CloudTrail is the account-wide record of who did what, when, and from where, across every AWS service — without it, there is no audit log to investigate an incident against, no way to answer 'was this bucket ever made public before today', and no evidence trail to hand a regulator or auditor. Most other findings in this tool describe a specific misconfigured resource; this one describes the absence of the record that would let anyone find out how it happened.
ACCOUNT_CLOUDTRAIL_DISABLED.remediation: Create a trail that logs to an S3 bucket the account controls and enable logging on it. In the AWS Console: CloudTrail -> Trails -> Create trail -> apply it to all regions -> choose or create a target S3 bucket -> Create. From the AWS CLI: `aws cloudtrail create-trail --name <name> --s3-bucket-name <bucket> --is-multi-region-trail` followed by `aws cloudtrail start-logging --name <name>`. A multi-region trail is strongly preferred over a single-region one, since it captures activity regardless of which region an attacker or a mistaken API call targets.

ACCOUNT_S3_BLOCK_PUBLIC_ACCESS_DISABLED.title: Account-level S3 Block Public Access not fully enabled
ACCOUNT_S3_BLOCK_PUBLIC_ACCESS_DISABLED.description: This is the account-wide version of the same Public Access Block safety net that bucket-level findings in this tool already check for individually. Set once at the account level, it overrides accidentally-public ACLs and bucket policies on every bucket in the account, including ones created after this setting was configured and any that individual bucket-level settings miss. Without it, protection depends entirely on every bucket being configured correctly on its own, every time, forever — one missed bucket is one public data exposure. This is the single highest-leverage S3 control available: one setting protects the whole account, present and future.
ACCOUNT_S3_BLOCK_PUBLIC_ACCESS_DISABLED.remediation: Enable all four account-level Public Access Block flags. In the AWS Console: S3 -> Block Public Access settings for this account -> Edit -> check 'Block all public access' -> Save. From the AWS CLI: `aws s3control put-public-access-block --account-id <account-id> --public-access-block-configuration BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true`. Buckets that legitimately serve public content should do so via CloudFront with an Origin Access Identity, not by leaving the account-level protection off to accommodate one bucket.
